brief.head: The universal outlaw
brief.text: Ajay Shah called him­self a con­ser­va­tive, be­cause he never wants so­cial en­gi­neer­ing, and a lib­eral, be­cause the world is a blank slate to re­think. {040-C15}

brief.head: A tube-light state
brief.text: Like slang’s tube light, slow on the up­take, the Indian state lags re­al­ity by ten or twenty years, Amit Varma said. Old in­sti­tu­tions, Ajay Shah agreed, are the bot­tle­neck. {040-C05}

brief.head: A reactor in a box
brief.text: Small mod­u­lar re­ac­tors, 50-megawatt black boxes for a fac­tory cor­ner, could let an alu­minium plant ex­port zero-carbon metal to Europe, Ajay Shah said. Liability rules stand in the way. {040-C12}

brief.head: Never read a report
brief.text: Reports are usu­ally bor­ing, Ajay Shah ad­mit­ted, but he called the International Energy Agency’s *World Energy Outlook 2023* un­put­down­able. The world of en­ergy, he said, “is pure drama today”. {040-R01}

brief.head: The red-eye discount
brief.text: Flexible power prices work like air­fares, Ajay Shah said: a red-eye or a mid­day flight is cheap, an 8 a.m. Bombay-Delhi flight dear, and peo­ple self-select. {#airfare}

thought.label: Thought for the day

thought.who: Ajay Shah, marvelling at the miracles of solar, wind and lighting

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the future of electricity
lead.head: Free at noon, costly at dusk

pic.caption: Ajay Shah (left) and Amit Varma in Episode 40

body: Electricity, Amit Varma said, is like water to a fish: so nor­mal that we no longer see it. So he in­vited lis­ten­ers to dive into a plug point and travel down the wire to see what lies at the other end. {040-S01}
Ajay Shah was the guide, and the jour­ney ran from coal plants to the price sys­tem, nu­clear re­ac­tors and India’s neigh­bours.
His the­sis: sci­ence has de­liv­ered mir­a­cles, and old in­sti­tu­tions have not caught up.
## The old world

In the old sys­tem, Shah said, the gov­ern­ment ran the grid. Demand from thou­sands of homes is smooth enough to fore­cast in 15-minute slots, and grid man­agers, like air traf­fic con­trollers, pick the cheap­est plant for each.
Coal plants need a cou­ple of hours to spin up or down, so sud­den swings fall to gas and hydel. Private gen­er­a­tors sat on 25-year con­tracts with fixed re­turns.
“It is not a world of busi­ness,” Shah said. “It is re­ally you’re just a can­teen con­trac­tor to the gov­ern­ment.” {040-C02}

Then came what he called “mir­a­cles upon mir­a­cles upon mir­a­cles”. Solar pan­els have got cheaper by 20 or 25 per cent a year for 30 years. Windmills went off­shore. LEDs took light­ing from ten per cent ef­fi­ciency to ninety.
## A cruel evening

The mir­a­cles broke the old grid. Solar floods it in the af­ter­noon. Demand peaks in the evening, when peo­ple come home to lights, air con­di­tion­ers and fridges whose com­pres­sors kick on, just as the sun goes away.
“The sun is a fickle friend,” Shah said. “He like mis­be­haves on you when you need him the most.” {040-J06}
Gas and hydel can­not cover the gap, and coal plants can­not be gunned all day. The plan­ners, he said, have no good an­swer.
## Let prices move
Shah’s an­swer was the price sys­tem. “When an econ­o­mist hears the word short­age, you think price,” he said. {040-C06}

Let af­ter­noon power fall to near zero, as it al­ready does on many sum­mer days in Germany, and let evening power go to 15, 25 or 50 ru­pees a unit. Nobody, he said, should whine about prof­i­teer­ing.

Then three things ad­just. Homes and firms shift their use to cheap hours. Wind, which blows after sun­set, earns the evening pre­mium. And stor­age, from bat­ter­ies to water pumped up­hill, be­comes a busi­ness that buys cheap and sells dear.
Is that anti-poor? No, the hosts said. Without prices there are short­ages, which the poor al­ready live with, and on av­er­age power would get cheaper.

Varma’s own pas­sion was nu­clear power. Coal smoke, he read from an essay co-written by Steven Pinker, kills more than half a mil­lion peo­ple a year, while sixty years of nu­clear deaths equal about one month of coal-related deaths. {040-R03}
Shah noted that India’s li­a­bil­ity rules mean not a sin­gle American or French re­ac­tor has ar­rived since the Indo-US nu­clear deal.

From there the wire led to Bhutan’s hydel, Nepal’s un­tapped hydel sites and off­shore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka. For Varma, the trip from a plug point to for­eign pol­icy was the show’s title, *Everything is Everything*, in ac­tion.
The same logic, Varma ar­gued, could price water and park­ing, and even save the tiger.

second.label: A 1971 rumour
second.head: The embargo that wasn’t
second.deck: Ajay Shah ran down a story of a 1971 oil cut-off. It never happened

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the rumoured 1971 oil cut-off

body: Growing up, Ajay Shah heard a vague claim: that dur­ing the Bangladesh war of 1971, the Middle Eastern states cut off India’s oil. It sup­pos­edly did not mat­ter only be­cause the war lasted 14 days and the Pakistani army sur­ren­dered. {#fourteenday}

The claim nagged at him. What if Saudi Arabia had been col­lud­ing with the United States? Something that big, he felt, could not be left as a vague al­le­ga­tion. So he reached a per­sonal friend of an Indian am­bas­sador to Saudi Arabia of a cer­tain pe­riod.
The an­swer: it never hap­pened. It was, Shah said, a ru­mour made up to por­tray those states as hos­tile to India. {040-S07} These, he said, are the ways a “toxic brew” can form.

quote.text: And I have it on full au­thor­ity that no, this never hap­pened.

third.head: First come, first parked

pic.caption: Amit Varma on free parking in Bombay

body: Amit Varma owns a small car that he rather likes. Yet in Bombay he often takes an Uber or pub­lic trans­port, be­cause he just won’t get park­ing. {#uber}

The ex­pla­na­tion came from his friends at Takshashila. The night be­fore record­ing, Varma had asked them for other uses of the price sys­tem. {040-S12} Nitin Pai said car park­ing: you have to price it. {#nitin}
Picture a wall, Varma said. On one side is the house, where real es­tate, es­pe­cially rent in Mumbai, is ex­or­bi­tant. On the other side is the road, where park­ing is free.
“It doesn’t make sense,” he said. “It means that who­ever can get in there gets in there.” Need does not mat­ter, and there are park­ing short­ages ev­ery­where.

from1.head: Free at noon, costly at dusk

photo.caption: David Foster Wallace at a Booksmith reading in 2006

box.title: The fish and the plug point
box.text: Amit Varma opened with David Foster Wallace’s para­ble of a fish who asks “What’s water?” The things we nor­malise, he said, be­come un­seen. Electricity is our water: we plug in, and it sim­ply works. {040-S01}

sections.label: The old world
sections.head: The grid’s canteen contractors
sections.caption: the grid’s old world
body: Before the mir­a­cles, Ajay Shah said, the grid was a gov­ern­ment af­fair. Big coal, gas and hydel plants sent power at high volt­age to sub­sta­tions, and on to every plug at 240 volts.

One house­hold switch­ing a TV on is ran­dom. Thousands of them can­cel out, much as an in­surer can pre­dict how many car crashes it will pay for each day. “By the time you get down to any kind of ge­o­graph­i­cal ag­gre­ga­tion,” Shah said, “then can­celling out hap­pens and there’s an in­sur­ance like char­ac­ter and it be­comes highly pre­dictable.” {040-C01}
So grid man­agers fore­cast de­mand in 15-minute slots, feed­ing in the weather and whether a cricket match is on, and choose the cheap­est plant for each.
## Slow coal

The catch is that coal plants need a cou­ple of hours to spin up or down. A sud­den cloudy evening in Bombay must be met by gas and hydel. Amit Varma claimed to have tried it: he asked a coal plant to spin up, and “it was very slow in re­spond­ing”. {040-J01}

Private gen­er­a­tors, Shah said, were mere ven­dors on 25-year con­tracts with fixed re­turns, doing no think­ing and tak­ing no risk. The gov­ern­ment did all the busi­ness think­ing, and the waste came back as ex­pen­sive elec­tric­ity. {040-C02}
~ Meanwhile, he said, “we the fat, in­do­lent, lazy in­grates of the world get this il­lu­sion that we just throw a switch and mag­i­cally the elec­tric­ity just hap­pens.” {040-J02}

quote.text: They are brave heroic peo­ple. We value their work. It’s like an air traf­fic con­troller.

sections.label: The problem
sections.head: Sunshine at the wrong hour
sections.caption: the sun’s cruel timing
body: Climate change, Ajay Shah said, set off an ex­plo­sion of re­search into en­ergy, and with it a run of sci­en­tific mir­a­cles.
Solar pan­els have grown cheaper at a com­pound rate of 20 or 25 per cent a year for 30 years. {#solar}

The sci­en­tist Shockley, one of the three Bell Labs in­ven­tors of the tran­sis­tor, had de­rived from quan­tum me­chan­ics a limit on how much sun­light a sil­i­con cell can con­vert. Shah re­mem­bered it as about twelve per cent. Engineers sim­ply tried other ma­te­ri­als and stacked them in lay­ers. {040-S03}
## Free money from the sky

On many sum­mer days in Germany, Shah said, the price of elec­tric­ity goes to zero, and Germany does not get much sun­light. India could have 250 to 275 days of bright sun. His favourite con­se­quence: charge your EV, and a backup bat­tery pack, free every af­ter­noon. {040-S06}

The catch comes at dusk. People get home and switch on lights, air con­di­tion­ers and TVs, and fridge com­pres­sors kick on. Just then the sun goes away, there is not enough gas and hydel, and coal can­not spin up in time. {040-C04}
~ The re­new­able rev­o­lu­tion, Shah said, had “messed with the sim­ple bor­ing pre­dictable Sarkari life of the old elec­tric­ity sys­tem”. Spare a thought, he urged, for the grid en­gi­neers.

quote.text: So at the worst pos­si­ble time, your best pos­si­ble source goes away. Like what could be more cruel than this?

portraits.caption: William Shockley
portraits.credit: Chuck Painter / Stanford News Service, CC BY 3.0

sections.label: The answer
sections.head: Shortage? Think price
sections.caption: letting the price move
body: Whenever you hear “rec­on­cile a gap be­tween sup­ply and de­mand”, Ajay Shah said, the an­swer is the price sys­tem. It was there “in the pages of Adam Smith in 1776”. {040-J17}

The grid en­gi­neer can only order sup­pli­ers about, be­cause con­sumers pay a fixed price. Both sides should ad­just. So let af­ter­noon power fall to 25 or 50 paise a unit, some­times zero, and let evening power climb to 15, 25 or 50 ru­pees a unit. {#evening}
## Three ad­just­ments

First, de­mand. People would glance at the spot price on their phones be­fore switch­ing on the AC. Firms would work a day shift and a night shift from 10 p.m. to 4 a.m., and close for the ex­pen­sive evening.
Second, wind, which keeps blow­ing after dark. The wind in­vestor, Shah said, would “make like a ban­dit in the evening when the price surge comes”. {040-C07}
Third, stor­age: bat­ter­ies, or water pumped from the Konkan up to the Sahyadris by day and re­leased as hydel power in the evening peak. “I’m a banya,” Shah said. “I’ll make money.”
~ None of this needs an en­gi­neer to pick the tech­nol­ogy mix, he ar­gued. Investors should take the risk, and go bank­rupt if they guess wrong. {040-C08}

quote.text: And no­body should whine. Nobody should say those guys are prof­i­teer­ing.

sections.label: The nuclear option
sections.head: Sixty years, one month
sections.caption: the case for nuclear power
body: Conventional think­ing on nu­clear power, Amit Varma said, is “so wrong”. People think of bombs, or of Chernobyl. He read in­stead from a *New York Times* essay, *Nuclear Power Can Save the World*, by three au­thors in­clud­ing Steven Pinker. {040-R03}
In 60 years of nu­clear power, it says, only three ac­ci­dents raised pub­lic alarm. Three Mile Island killed no one. Chernobyl was the re­sult of “ex­tra­or­di­nary Soviet bungling”.

Sixty years of American nu­clear waste would fit in one Walmart. {#walmart} France gets about 71 per cent of its elec­tric­ity from nu­clear, Varma said, and its car­bon per kilo­watt-hour is a tenth of the rest of the world’s. {#france}
## Weapons and watts

Ajay Shah drew a line. India’s nu­clear jour­ney, from Homi Bhabha to Indira Gandhi and Pokhran, was a na­tion­al­ist weapons project, and that story, he said, is over. Nuclear en­ergy should be pri­vate, com­pet­i­tive, global cap­i­tal­ism. {040-C11}
At the fi­nance min­istry, he had re­alised that the Kalpakkam fa­cil­ity, its costs reck­oned cor­rectly, was not com­pet­i­tive. Indian re­ac­tors were “a sci­ence project”. {040-S08}
~ Yet India holds for­eign ven­dors li­able for­ever for any ac­ci­dent. “It’s like say­ing I sold you a car and thirty years from now you had an ac­ci­dent and I’m re­spon­si­ble,” Shah said.

quote.text: If you care about the en­vi­ron­ment, if you care about cli­mate change, you should em­brace nu­clear.

sections.label: Foreign policy
sections.head: Good neighbours, cheap power
sections.caption: power and the neighbours
body: Markets gain from larger net­works, Amit Varma said, and na­tion­al­ism shrinks them. Ajay Shah agreed: for­eign pol­icy is not for pro­pa­ganda or scor­ing de­bat­ing points at the United Nations, but for deals that serve the in­ter­ests of the peo­ple of India. {040-C13}

Bhutan is the suc­cess. India spends mil­i­tary and diplo­matic ef­fort shield­ing it from Chinese in­cur­sions, as Doklam in 2017 showed. In re­turn, Indian firms build and run hydel plants there, send the power home and pay Bhutan rent for the sites. {040-S10}
Nepal is the fail­ure. Its glaciers melt in sum­mer just as North India runs its air con­di­tion­ers, but toxic fights over its con­sti­tu­tion and a Hindu state have bro­ken the re­la­tion­ship.
## Tamil Nadu’s North Sea

The third prize is off­shore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, which Shah likened to the North Sea’s oil and gas for Britain. Electricity is a state sub­ject, so Tamil Nadu must first build evening peak prices and mar­kets, not flat 25-year con­tracts. “It is theirs to win, it is theirs to lose.” {040-S11}

~ Then India must mend ties with Sri Lanka, so Indian firms can build on Sri Lankan sites and bring the power ashore. The good Lord, Shah said, was telling both coun­tries to “get your shit to­gether”. {040-J12}

quote.text: There is no bet­ter deal in the world than gen­er­at­ing Himalayan hydel elec­tric­ity and send­ing it into the Indian Hindi heart­land

sections.label: Beyond the grid
sections.head: Water, parking and tigers
sections.caption: prices in sacred places
body: Ajay Shah asked Amit Varma where else the price sys­tem solves prob­lems in ways peo­ple don’t in­tuit. Varma had polled his friends at Takshashila.

Water came first. Anupam Manur, who teaches eco­nom­ics at Takshashila, had writ­ten about Bangalore’s water short­age and ar­gued for pric­ing water. The poor are suf­fer­ing any­way, Varma said, and today’s sys­tem favours the rich, who use far more of it. {040-R06}
Every in­ter­fer­ence with the price sys­tem, he ar­gued, ef­fec­tively re­dis­tributes wealth from the poor to the rich.
## Sell the tiger

His friend Barun Mitra, Varma re­called, wrote in the *New York Times*, he thought in the early 2000s, that sell­ing tigers should be legal. People would then breed them, as they breed cows and chick­ens, and save the species. {040-R10}

Garbage col­lec­tion could be pri­va­tised and organ sales al­lowed, Varma said. Shah added the mak­ers of COVID vac­cines, who he said were not paid in line with the tril­lions of dol­lars they added to world GDP, and sur­ro­gacy, where “the Indian state has come along and banned ev­ery­thing”. {#vaccines}
~ Agriculture and ed­u­ca­tion suf­fer, Varma said, be­cause the state keeps the mar­ket out of them. {040-C14}

quote.text: The an­swer ev­ery­where is prices be­cause prices are so pow­er­ful in the way that they carry in­for­ma­tion and in­cen­tives.
The pur­pose of for­eign pol­icy is to make deals with gov­ern­ments of other coun­tries in the way that best suits the in­ter­ests of the peo­ple of India. It is about in­ter­ests.

p3.title: Tales of the grid
p3.deck: Windmills, light bulbs, an emperor and a prime minister, as the hosts told them

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on how a simple machine went to sea
stories.head: Up, up and out to sea
body: A wind­mill sounds sim­ple. How com­pli­cated can it be? You would think, Ajay Shah said, that all the ge­nius of aero­nau­ti­cal en­gi­neer­ing that fig­ured out the pro­pel­ler would do the job.

Then watch the in­no­va­tions. First, en­gi­neers wanted to get off the ground, be­cause the wind is stronger up there. Anyone who has flown a kite knows it strug­gles near the ground and then finds pow­er­ful winds higher up.
“Hello Viral and Vikram,” Shah said in pass­ing, not­ing that you can put a dozen can­dles on a kite that climbs a kilo­me­tre or two.

Taller wind­mills needed big­ger blades, which made it a prob­lem of ma­te­ri­als sci­ence: giant blades that are light and strong, will not break, and last 25 years. The sci­en­tists went and did that.

Then, in Shah’s telling, they grew un­happy. “I’m trapped by the surly bonds of earth. I want to go even higher. I want big­ger, bet­ter, more.” So they went off­shore, where the flat sea gives an even stronger wind and room for even big­ger ma­chines. {040-S04}

The next chal­lenge was a blade about 100 me­tres on each side. {#blade} Steel py­lons go into the seabed of India’s shal­low coastal shelf, a 200-metre wind­mill whirs above, and the elec­tric­ity is car­ried back to land.
~ Amit Varma later pointed out that Shah had used a Chennai slang word with­out know­ing it: blade, mean­ing damn bor­ing. Shah, he said, is the op­po­site of blade. {040-J03}
stories.why: Big en­gi­neer­ing leaps, Shah’s tale sug­gests, come as chains of solved prob­lems: taller tow­ers needed big­ger blades, and the hunger for more took wind­mills out to sea. Each an­swer opened the way to the next.
stories.postscript: Offshore wind off Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka, Shah said later, is India’s North Sea. {040-S11}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the windmill that kept climbing

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the magic we no longer notice
stories.head: Switch on, your majesty
body: Get into a time ma­chine, Ajay Shah sug­gested, and visit Akbar, the most pow­er­ful ruler of the Middle Ages. Tell him you can plug some­thing in, flick a switch, and “all kinds of magic hap­pens”. {040-S02}
“It’s magic, okay?” Shah said. Sufficiently ad­vanced tech­nol­ogy, he added, is in­dis­tin­guish­able from magic. {040-J15}

And yet we take it for granted. We have be­come “dumb users”, he said: we flick a switch, the elec­tric­ity flows and is me­tered, and a bill ar­rives at the end of the month. In some parts of India, he added, peo­ple steal it in­stead.
~ Behind the switch stand coal, gas and hydel plants, lines that carry power at high volt­age to keep losses down, and sub­sta­tions that bring it to every plug at 240 volts.
stories.why: By the stan­dards of his­tory, an or­di­nary house­hold com­mands pow­ers no em­peror ever had, and barely no­tices. Amit Varma made the same point with a fish that asks, “What’s water?” {040-S01}

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on Akbar and the light switch

stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the quiet revolution in lighting
stories.head: The bulb that was a heater
body: Ajay Shah is old enough, he said, to re­mem­ber when bulbs were cool and the puz­zle was mak­ing them last. Bulbs kept blow­ing, so their case was filled with a noble gas to stop the hot tung­sten fil­a­ment from ox­i­dis­ing.
Tube lights came next, giv­ing the same light more ef­fi­ciently. Then came the LED rev­o­lu­tion.

“So roughly speak­ing in a tung­sten bulb, ten per­cent of the en­ergy goes out as light, ninety per­cent goes out as heat,” Shah said. “It’s ac­tu­ally a heater.” {040-S05} An LED, by con­trast, reaches ninety per cent ef­fi­ciency. {#led}

~ White LED light needed blue LEDs first, which Shah said great Japanese sci­en­tists at the University of California at Santa Barbara fig­ured out. The ex­otic, ex­pen­sive tech­nol­ogy was then mass-produced. Today LED bulbs are ev­ery­where in India.
stories.why: The en­ergy rev­o­lu­tion is not only about new ways to make power. Wasting less of it counts too: going from ten per cent ef­fi­ciency to ninety was, in Shah’s words, “just mirac­u­lous gain”.

pic.caption: Ajay Shah on the tungsten bulb

stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a prime minister’s stand, and its sour coda
stories.head: Prime minister, or no deal
body: Amit Varma has long ad­mired the nu­clear deal that Manmohan Singh pushed through with George W. Bush. The Left par­ties were against it, and Sonia Gandhi did not want it. {040-S09}
Singh put his po­lit­i­cal sur­vival at stake. “Manmohan took a firm stand and said that I will not be prime min­is­ter if I can­not do this be­cause it’s good for the coun­try,” Varma said.

Ajay Shah sup­plied the back­drop: the Indian es­tab­lish­ment was pro-Soviet. The rap­proche­ment with America came from lead­ers like Narasimha Rao, Vajpayee, Jaswant Singh and Manmohan Singh, not the bu­reau­cracy. {#rapprochement}

~ The coda is sour. Liability rules mean not one American or French re­ac­tor has ar­rived since. Varma likened it to hold­ing Hyundai li­able for every ac­ci­dent he might ever have: “It is ab­surd, it is bizarre.”
stories.why: Leaders can break in­sti­tu­tional in­er­tia, the story sug­gests, but a rule fur­ther down the line can qui­etly undo the win. India’s li­a­bil­ity rules, Shah said, have “negated the essence of the nu­clear deal”. {#negated}

pic.caption: Amit Varma on Manmohan Singh’s stand

quiz.q: What limit did Shockley derive, and how did engineers get round it?
quiz.a: A cap on sil­i­con cells’ ef­fi­ciency; en­gi­neers tried other ma­te­ri­als and stacked lay­ers.

quiz.q: Why did Ajay Shah call the old tungsten bulb a heater?
quiz.a: Ten per cent of its en­ergy goes out as light, ninety per cent as heat.

quiz.q: What happens to the price of electricity on many summer days in Germany?
quiz.a: It falls to zero, be­cause there is so much solar ca­pac­ity there.

quiz.q: In the Bhutan hydel deal, what does India bring and what does Bhutan get?
quiz.a: Indian firms build and run the plants and take the power; Bhutan gets rent.

quiz.q: Why does Amit Varma often take an Uber in Bombay despite owning a car?
quiz.a: Roadside park­ing is free, so who­ever gets there first takes it, and he finds none.

quiz.q: By the essay Varma read, sixty years of nuclear deaths equal how many coal deaths?
quiz.a: About one month of coal-related deaths, even al­low­ing for claimed Chernobyl cover-ups.

p4.credits: Everything is Everything was Amit Varma and Ajay Shah’s weekly show, 128 episodes from June 2023 to December 2025. This edition is made from Episode 40. The moving pictures, stills and chapter cards are from its video; the chapter art is by Simahina. Every play button starts the video at the moment it was said. The articles and headlines were written by Claude, an AI model, from the episode’s machine-made transcript, and checked against it. Other photographs are from Wikimedia Commons: Manmohan Singh (Prime Minister’s Office, GODL-India); David Foster Wallace (Steve Rhodes, CC BY 2.0); William Shockley (Chuck Painter / Stanford News Service, CC BY 3.0); Adam Smith (Wikimedia Commons, public domain); Steven Pinker (Christopher Michel, CC BY-SA 4.0); Frédéric Bastiat (Émile Desmaisons. Lithograph by Auguste-Hilaire Léveillé., public domain). The covers on the shelf are from Amazon.

shelf.title: World Energy Outlook 2023
shelf.creator: International Energy Agency
shelf.why: He ad­mits peo­ple flee from re­ports as bor­ing of­fi­cial plat­i­tudes, but calls this one un­put­down­able.

shelf.title: Midnight in Chernobyl
shelf.creator: Adam Higginbotham
shelf.why: Gripping re­portage on what hap­pened be­hind the scenes at Chernobyl, show­ing the dis­as­ter as a fail­ure of the Soviet state, rooted in its struc­ture and in­cen­tives so that it seems bound to hap­pen.

shelf.title: Nuclear Power Can Save the World
shelf.creator: Joshua S Goldstein, Staffan A Qvist & Steven Pinker
shelf.why: The data be­hind the hosts’ case for nu­clear power: sixty years of nu­clear deaths, Chernobyl in­cluded, roughly equal one month of coal-related deaths, and 60 years of American nu­clear waste could fit in a sin­gle Walmart.

shelf.title: That Which is Seen, and That Which is Not Seen
shelf.creator: Frédéric Bastiat
shelf.why: Bastiat’s bro­ken-window para­ble, which teaches you to look past a policy’s vis­i­ble ef­fect to its un­seen costs and in­tro­duced op­por­tu­nity cost decades be­fore the term ex­isted.

shelf.title: This is Water
shelf.creator: David Foster Wallace
shelf.why: Its para­ble, where a fish asks ‘what’s water?’, cap­tures how the things we nor­malise be­come in­vis­i­ble.

shelf.title: Anupam Manur’s piece on the Bangalore water crisis
shelf.creator: Anupam Manur
shelf.why: Amit urges ev­ery­one to read it be­cause it is so coun­ter­in­tu­itive.

shelf.title: Making Policy Fun with Khyati Pathak and Friends (Episode 374, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Khyati Pathak, Anupam Manur and Pranay Kotasthane
shelf.why: A con­ver­sa­tion with Takshashila friends that in­cludes Anupam Manur’s case for pric­ing water, the same logic this episode ap­plies to elec­tric­ity.

shelf.title: The Great Redistribution
shelf.creator: Amit Varma
shelf.why: Amit’s ar­gu­ment that mar­ket in­ter­ven­tions such as tar­iffs or bans on FDI in re­tail qui­etly move money from many dis­persed, poor con­sumers to a few or­gan­ised, rich in­ter­est groups, the op­po­site of their stated in­ten­tion.

shelf.title: Pranay Kotasthane’s post on plasma and organ sales
shelf.creator: Pranay Kotasthane
shelf.why: Pranay lays out the eco­nomic logic for al­low­ing sales and how it works in other parts of the world.

shelf.title: Sell the Tiger to Save It
shelf.creator: Barun Mitra
shelf.why: Barun Mitra’s ar­gu­ment, against the re­flex to ban ev­ery­thing, that le­gal­is­ing the tiger trade would give peo­ple a rea­son to breed tigers as they breed cows and chick­ens, and so save the species.

shelf.title: Solving the intermittency of renewables
shelf.creator: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Deeper read­ing on the episode’s cen­tral puz­zle: how to cope when solar dis­ap­pears ex­actly as evening de­mand surges.

shelf.title: Offshore wind in Tamil Nadu: from potential to reality
shelf.creator: Akshay Jaitly, Charmi Mehta, Renuka Sane & Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The de­tailed case be­hind Ajay’s claim that Tamil Nadu must build the pol­icy ca­pa­bil­ity to un­lock off­shore wind.

shelf.title: A new dawn for nuclear energy?
shelf.creator: Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay’s writ­ing on nu­clear en­ergy, be­hind his op­ti­mism and his ar­gu­ment for sep­a­rat­ing nu­clear weapons from nu­clear power and treat­ing re­ac­tors as a busi­ness.

shelf.title: Climate Change and Our Power Sector (Episode 278, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Akshay Jaitly and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Akshay Jaitly and Ajay on cli­mate change and India’s power sec­tor, cen­tred on the elec­tric­ity grid: the con­ver­sa­tional ver­sion of their case for re­form­ing elec­tric­ity.

shelf.title: What’s Wrong With Indian Agriculture? (Episode 18, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Why Indian farm­ing, which em­ploys 40 to 60% of Indians against about 5% in rich coun­tries, is held back by the lack of a work­ing price sys­tem: MSPs that favour ce­re­als over pulses, loan waivers in­stead of struc­tural re­form, gluts and col­laps­ing prices.

shelf.title: India’s Agriculture Crisis (Episode 140, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Barun Mitra & Kumar Anand
shelf.why: Barun Mitra and Kumar Anand on agri­cul­ture as a field where the state con­trols ev­ery­thing and farm­ers suf­fer, in­clud­ing the year MSPs were promised for 24 com­modi­ties but paid for only six.

shelf.title: The Tragedy of Our Farm Bills (Episode 211, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah
shelf.why: Ajay and Amit on India’s farm bills, which would have kept APMCs but given farm­ers the choice to sell else­where, and on why farm re­form keeps stalling.

shelf.title: The State of Our Farmers (Episode 86, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Gunvant Patil
shelf.why: A Hindi-language con­ver­sa­tion with Gunvant Patil on the con­di­tion of Indian farm­ers, which Amit calls ‘a mas­ter­piece of illumination’: farm­ers stat­ing free-market ideas drawn from lived ex­pe­ri­ence.

shelf.title: Fixing Indian Education (Episode 185, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Karthik Muralidharan
shelf.why: A deep dive with Karthik Muralidharan into what’s bro­ken in Indian ed­u­ca­tion and how to fix it, in­clud­ing his point that the sys­tem is op­ti­mised for sort­ing, not teach­ing.

shelf.title: Education in India (Episode 77, The Seen and the Unseen)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma with Amit Chandra
shelf.why: An ear­lier long-form con­ver­sa­tion with Amit Chandra on the state of Indian ed­u­ca­tion, an­other field the hosts say suf­fers from keep­ing prices out.

shelf.title: We Love Vaccines! We Love Freedom! (Episode 27, Everything is Everything)
shelf.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
shelf.why: The third part of the state se­ries, ap­ply­ing its tool­kit to vac­cines: COVID vac­cine mak­ers were paid far less than the value they cre­ated, and let­ting prices rise would al­lo­cate vac­cines bet­ter and fund re­search for the next pan­demic.

shelf.title: Son of Bosey
shelf.creator: Anand Ramachandran
shelf.why: The great blog of Anand Ramachandran, whom Amit calls per­haps the fun­ni­est man in Indian his­tory.

laughs.text: After Ajay de­scribes ask­ing a coal plant to spin up, Amit dead­pans: ‘I went to a coal power plant and I said, Hey dude, I need you to spin up and you’re right, it was very slow in re­spond­ing. I didn’t hang around for a cou­ple of hours to see if it started re­spond­ing.’

Ajay on con­sumers who think power just ap­pears: ‘we the fat, in­do­lent, lazy in­grates of the world get this il­lu­sion that we just throw a switch and mag­i­cally the elec­tric­ity just hap­pens.’

Amit points out that Ajay un­know­ingly used two slang words, ‘blade’ (wind­mill blades) and ‘tube light’. ‘Blade’ is Chennai slang for damn bor­ing, learned from Anand Ramachandran, ‘the fun­ni­est man in Indian history’. Ajay is the op­po­site of blade, mak­ing en­gi­neer­ing so fun Amit would have wanted to be one: ‘Thank God I wasn’t.’ And when it comes to Amit’s bad jokes, Ajay is a tube light: ‘You get them the next day.’
Ajay day­dream­ing of free af­ter­noon power in India: ‘imag­ine there are no pol­icy mis­takes. It’s easy if you try.’
Ajay on solar’s evening dis­ap­pear­ance: ‘the sun is a fickle friend. He like mis­be­haves on you when you need him the most.’

Amit, after Ajay mocks gov­ern­ment can­teen con­trac­tors: ‘some of my clos­est friends are gov­ern­ment can­teen con­trac­tors. You know, they make great medu vadas. They will be very of­fended at see­ing this episode.’

Amit bor­rows Ajay’s ‘Hey, Mr. Gas’ for TV news: ‘every time I watch news tele­vi­sion and I see some ran­dom ex­pert spout­ing yarn on some­thing, I feel like say­ing to him, Hey, Mr. Gas. Shut the fuck up.’

After Ajay de­scribes small mod­u­lar re­ac­tors as black boxes in a fac­tory cor­ner, Amit says: ‘I’ve been in your dinky lit­tle Mumbai flat, and one third of the flat is taken up by this big black box. Is it a re­ac­tor?’

Ajay casts the off­shore wind op­por­tu­nity as di­vine ex­as­per­a­tion: the good Lord putting a bounty off the coast and say­ing ‘India, Sri Lanka, get your shit to­gether. I’m giv­ing you such a big prize, if only you will un­der­stand how to work to­gether.’

The episode’s arc, from a plug point all the way to for­eign pol­icy with Sri Lanka, is Amit’s live il­lus­tra­tion of the show’s title: ‘Like who would have thought that you’re going to get into a plug point... and end up with for­eign pol­icy.’
Ajay chan­nels the line ‘suf­fi­ciently ad­vanced tech­nol­ogy is in­dis­tin­guish­able from magic’, imag­in­ing show­ing a light switch to Akbar.
Adam Smith: ‘the amaz­ing so­lu­tion, the re­mark­able so­lu­tion, was in the pages of Adam Smith in 1776’, namely let prices move.
G.K. Gokhale, Ranade and Agarkar, the free­dom-struggle lib­er­als Amit claims as he­roes of ‘lib­eral ends but con­ser­va­tive means’.
Amit on the Indian state of the Chernobyl era: ‘in many ways was a fax copy of what the Soviet state was’.
